results.summary_before: This is a 4-bit vector multiplication engine that multiplies two vectors of up to 32 elements and accumulates the result into an 8-bit output. It is programmed via a register interface using read/write opcodes and a run command, and it operates in two clock cycles. The design is intended to be controlled by an RP2040 and requires no other external hardware. Silicon tests show it works, though timing adjustments were needed.

results.summary_before: This project reads input from a Gamepad PMOD and displays the pressed buttons as green symbols on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout and a 25.175 MHz clock, and is intended to be run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board with both PMODs attached. After reset, pressing a gamepad button causes its corresponding symbol to appear on screen. It is a demonstration of combining the Gamepad and Tiny VGA PMODs, derived from the VGA Playground, and needs both external PMOD boards to operate.

results.summary_before: This project implements a stream cipher using an 8-byte linear shift register to encrypt and decrypt messages. It accepts 8-bit data on input pins and uses bidirectional pins for control signals such as increment, encrypt, and view mode. The encrypted or decrypted message can be viewed by selecting an index, and the design supports toggling between encryption and viewing without resetting. Notable limitations include the need to reset after 16 bytes to avoid losing encrypted data, and the documentation provides clear testing steps.

results.summary_before: This design implements a perceptron that reads two 8-bit inputs and computes a weighted sum with fixed 8-bit weights, classifying the result as 1 if it exceeds a threshold of 11111110 and 0 otherwise. The documentation explains the math with examples, such as any input with two or more 1s being classified as 1, and credits a UCSC professor. It is intended as a simple 9+10 adder or perceptron demonstration, and testing involves applying inputs and observing the 8-bit output. The design is notable for being an educational neuromorphic example with clear documentation.

results.summary_before: This project is a 15-channel pulse counter designed for acoustic emission detection, counting short digital pulses on each channel and periodically outputting the counts serially. It includes a real-time clock (RTC) for time-stamping, overflow detection, and a readout state machine. The design is an early work-in-progress test implementation and is the second Tiny Tapeout submission, improving on a previous 4-channel version. External hardware such as a logic analyzer is recommended for debugging.

results.summary_before: This project is a test structure for a future register file macro, implemented as an SRAM with one write port and two read ports. It is not designed for use with the demo board but instead requires a dedicated test platform, ideally using FPGA hardware to drive control signals with precise timing. Silicon test reports from the author indicate that the memory works correctly, with tens of thousands of random read/write cycles passing, but timing characterization is incomplete due to limitations of the RP2040 controller. The design is notable as a successful early test of a memory macro, though further testing is needed.
